segments.verbatim: I'm extremely worried. I try to limit my kids' screen time.

You look at Stanford — they teach UX designers basically how to create more sticky, addictive interfaces. So you're seeing an entire generation of software that's already been developed, a paradigm that's already been institutionalized in social media, where it's just designed to maximize attention.
And now you're throwing algorithmic design into that design paradigm — basically creating a really dangerous mechanism.
As a parent of two and as somebody who really cares a lot about my students, there's no defensibility here. So I am very, very worried about it.
I do believe that we are losing our cognitive ability to critically problem-solve.
One of my biggest concerns is that I don't see students who can read a book cover to cover — because they don't have the focus, or "oh, I don't read," or something like that.
That's indicative of somebody who can't focus and concentrate and do the cognitive lifting necessary to be successful out in the world.
I just don't think that we're developing a generation of students who have patience — because something is instantly available to them.
Like the animators I've talked about: "what's your favorite movie?" They don't watch Pixar movies anymore. They scroll TikTok because everything is algorithmically chopped up and fed to them.
My first take is not that we need more AI in our curriculum. I think we actually need to have the mechanisms to make people understand that it is dangerous — the way that drugs are dangerous.
People should go outside. They should learn to disconnect. And then they should engage intentionally, with real presence, with technology.
I do use AI to write, but I also spend a long time outlining, thinking, structuring ideas together. I try not to let AI pick that process for me.

I always keep a sketchbook, or I always keep a notebook — and what it does is it helps me synthesize the material that I've learned. It also gives me a record so I can say, "oh, how did I do that thing?"
The way that you would go to the gym or go for a run to keep your physical self up — I think you need to do the same thing with your mental self.

I really think we should institutionalize the practice of devlogs — recording your process, self-reflection. "Why am I building this thing? Where am I going to be next week? Did I look back — last week, did I accomplish what I did?"
Nathan Madrid, who is the new Applied AI professor, has been teaching and he came [to me] and was like, "we don't even have an approach for any of this ethical stuff."
Since he's teaching agentic workflows, he's been working on trying to create agentic markdown files that would embed [ethics constraints] in the agentic closure.

SCAD's not really doing this, but I believe we're going to have to build it — we're probably going to have to get someone else's infrastructure because we don't have the technical capability to do this ourselves.
Regardless of what model wins, there's going to be a layer of infrastructure in every educational program. I hope it's open source, because it should be accessible to everyone.
It's going to have those structures so that when a query comes in, you have those guardrails in place: "Are you cheating? Is this actually your work? Are you citing your sources correctly?"

We can absolutely talk about these things in the classroom — "are you being honest? Are you actually doing these things?" — but everybody just has the tendency to cheat or cut corners. So I think we need to have those infrastructures in place.

The long-term approach is that we just need to be better humans. We need to spend more time with each other in communities. We need to be going outside. We need to learn how to unplug. And we also need to fundamentally question how we build software from an ethical perspective.
In the short term, I think that our defensibility is devlogs every week, and some sort of agentic systems that police our IP and cheating and all that kind of stuff.

I just had a roboticist blow up at me, because she got emotional. I've had this reaction from multiple people. At a certain point you realize there are huge ethical issues — choose one of them, just choose one — and it's an emotional roller coaster.
My most recent blog post — I talked about the AI bubble, and I sort of soft-pitched this, but I actually really believe it: I want it to pop.
It's sort of like nuclear, right? It's only after we saw Chernobyl and Hiroshima that we were like, "what should we be doing this? Is this a really good idea?"

My greatest concern is that we're going to screw up the minds of an entire generation of humans. It's not actually going to be something blowing up or whatever — it's going to be just, like, structurally dangerous for society. A slow…

I am increasingly worried about sycophancy. I've gone through these emotional debates, and I've been using AI, and I realize it's only reflecting whatever I'm saying at that emotional moment. If you're like, "you know, I hate this thing," it's going to give you all the data necessary to follow that pattern.

So it's not actually giving us the ability to critically weigh ideas. It's actually supporting your insane conspiracy, the opportunity to go off on this different path. What's happening is — you're going to fracture society way more than you even expect.

It's hard for me, increasingly, to get excited about it. I'm supposed to build this School of Creative Technology. I introduced the Applied AI program, and I said one of the pillars is impact — I wanted every student to understand they have to measure the impact of their actions.

"You can't have my name on this. Okay, bye-bye. This cat doesn't care. It's like a money machine." And so: "hey, I need to hire this ethics thing." "Well, you know, we don't want to." But "oh, we gotta get robots. Let's make sure we get robots."

The person who actively wants to do ethics with this is Violetta. She's passionate about it. I'm like, "we should give it to her." So I empowered her. And what did she do? She created all these constraints in government and governance systems, and everyone was like, "oh, she's always blocking things." And I was like, "yeah, she's blocking things because she's ethically driven."
I'm trying really hard to make good on this, but I'm compromised — because what's the next shiny thing that we're doing? No one wants to do the Debbie Downer and have your ethics class.

Another crisis I'm losing sleep over is civics. If you go, like, the city of Savannah — it has no technical infrastructure. Are we going to let Amazon just come in with autonomous vehicles, or NVIDIA, and set up the thing? All of our data is just going to wind up in centralized servers.

This is what happened with electricity — electricity was a huge debate. Was this going to be owned by a series of [monopolies]? Even Georgia Power is a monopoly. Are we actually going to create a public utility with people we vote for, to maximize the well-being of the community? Or are we going to have one centralized actor who can charge anything they want, and then we're all going to be beholden to [them]?

Already — if you look at Savannah, watch the neighborhoods that are suffering: the ones that are Black, the ones that are flooding-prone. It's basically going to skew towards "can you afford AI?" and continue to keep Amazon and whoever in [control]. Can you pay for that? Because we are not actually democratizing it.

He sent me this guy who had this theory that the current AI is like the subprime mortgage crisis. If you think about OpenAI or Claude — now you have an entire ecosystem of startups and applications built on these centralized models. Which means they're paying inferencing costs to centralized actors.

The cost of AI might be dropping, but because we're doing more and more services, we're actually spending three hundred bucks a month, five hundred bucks a month. These companies that started off with inferencing costs of a hundred thousand are now paying a million, seven million, twenty million, billions.
Essentially, you're feeding all of your possibility to centralized actors. So if the bubble pops, you have an entire infrastructure of AI companies that are just going to collapse.

Look at what's happening in the Ukraine war. Could you imagine once we have completely democratized drone warfare? The danger is just insane. I would rather have this drop out now, have a step back, and be like — I would like us to survive.

I have ninety things that I have to do right now. By Monday I'm gonna have to have what we talked about in robotics, and I'm also going to have to deal with what we're doing with the schedule in ITGM. I'm going to do it, and at [a] certain point I'm just going to cheat my way because I need to get through it faster.
If somebody is asking me "hey, really, really think about this," but you're out of time and I've got ninety things to do, whatever — I cheat. It's human nature. So this is hard.

Number one: blog every week. I force myself to do that, because I know that if I don't spend the time thinking about what am I going to say, what am I going to think about what I'm going to do — I won't.
I also read books with pages, and I dedicate time to that, and I deliberately unplug.
It's sort of like — you can't get drunk every night. If you get drunk every night, the long-term effects are: you're going to completely destroy yourself.

It has to be like: how are you keeping yourself healthy? Same way cognitively: are you continuing to read books, or continuing to write, or continuing to think about things? Are you talking to humans?

[Prof.] Cody is also equally concerned. Dr. Tannen is super concerned about the cognitive decline of our students — she comes to me regularly with data. She's managing classes and coming to me saying, "look at this drop."

I also came from Macon, where I was talking to a whole bunch of STEM fairs — we're doing great with elementary schools [with] technology. And so — [that cohort] winds up as a freshman in my class exactly.
I think there are a lot of faculty who are just concerned about cognitive decline. I think very few of them put it together the same way.

There's sort of a movement amongst the students now toward indie gaming, and in the gaming program there's an increase in the use of vibe coding to do this — which I think is interesting, because it was all "no AI, I'm not going to have any AI in my game development." But now they're kind of saying, "oh, but coding's okay — but not art."
What does that mean to the art form? What is the true value of anything?

What that makes me do is — I get up in the morning and I see my kids. I'm going to make sure that I sit with them, and I have breakfast in the morning, and I walk them out the door and put them on the bus. And then I'm also going to take thirty minutes every day to write on my blog, because I think that's more important.
If it's the end of the world, I would rather have spent that time with my kids. And even if it's not the end of the world, I still think it's probably better for me to spend more time with my kids.

The city of Savannah reached out to me. I'm going to be on a board with the city controller [and others]. We've now got to a point where the city of Savannah has recognized that we need to have some sort of strategy for dealing with AI.
Everything SCAD is [doing] — it's just almost terrifying [compared to] other schools. Other [institutions] are governing people.

The [Savannah] port fought vehemently "no AI, no robotics. We want to defend our jobs for the next ten years." They signed off on all these things: "not using AI, not using robotics." The truth is, you look at their usage on their computers — they're all using AI.

I cannot shake that book from my brain. That is why I spend every morning with my kids. I am absolutely terrified that TikTok — and whatever the fuck we're doing right now — is just going to destroy the humanity that we know, and I'm not even going to recognize what's going to happen in the evening.

South by Southwest — I was with [someone] from one of the big AI / autonomous vehicle teams, a buddy of mine now. He does the autonomous vehicle pipeline. He is almost uninspired, and how impressed he is — he's seeing the AI models, seeing how quickly it's going. He's basically in an ethical crisis because he doesn't want to be in that space anymore.
I basically was like, "guys, we can't be [that]. We've gotta fight." I said, "I've gotta be like Aragorn — like Frodo — and run right into it."
The truth is — if the NVIDIA guys are starting to be depressed, we really have to fight.
Honestly, it's completely everything for me. From my undergrad — process, making — it's changed my process.
The way I was taught in undergrad: my undergrad is in Digital Media Design. Process-making and problem-solving — I was taught to problem-solve by myself.
Outreach through research and YouTube videos, teaching myself to problem-solve.

When 3D modeling or animating or graphic-designing, if I didn't know how to use a tool, I knew how to problem-solve that through researching and finding videos online that re-taught me how to do that.
That was the greatest thing that I could have been taught in my undergrad.
I actually went back and talked to my professor about that when I graduated last year — told him, and talked to my classmates about that being the best thing that we could have been taught.
And then, when I came to [grad] school, I honestly have been disappointed in the amount of AI usage — because I don't think it's necessary.
Too much. We're using it too much — because I don't think it's necessary to implement it into every process that we're doing.
I don't think all of our classes are doing it, but one of my classes that I'm taking right now — for instance — it is implemented into every process.
I am making an app right now. I know how to make an app from beginning to finish without using AI, but I'm being forced to implement AI by my professor because of the workflow he wants us to use.
It's not necessary. It's only necessary for his outcome that he wants.

I'm having issues with it, because this is an art and design school. I understand from SCAD's perspective — we are a fast-paced program that also pushes us to work very well in the work field. So I get it to a certain extent.

But at the same time — in my favorite perspective — I want to be taught how to use my software and my programs traditionally first. That way, if anything stops working, I can count on myself. I can rely on myself to do it.
That's where my problems reside in a lot of the AI usage — also with just my own morals and ethics. I know a lot of people have that issue.

As a student, I've also been going back and forth in my head: "What am I doing in my career?" My career is completely changed from when I started to now. And then I'm like, "okay, well, what am I doing in school? I'm not doing the same thing that I started versus now." Every day, I'm having a mental battle.
Some of my professors I respect — I love the way they are implementing it. And then this class I'm taking — I'm really resenting it. Because it's MVP, but it's online.

I've been wondering if people around me are having the same issue I am. I was talking to one of my friends yesterday, and we were both having the same internal struggle — "where the hell is AI going? Where does this leave us, and what do we do?"
I know to my core: I'm a designer. I'm an artist. I want to help people. I don't want to follow a machine.
My goal, my career, was — "I'm going to do what makes me happiest, and I'm not falling from that path just because there's new technology."

I don't know that everybody feels the same way, and that scares me. I think a lot of people probably feel that way, but they don't feel confident enough to talk about it — because nobody knows what to do.
Two.
No — we are open, because our course is literally AI-focused, and our professor, I mean, he's obsessed with AI. He loves it. I've never met someone — it drives me crazy.

I really liked him in the beginning. As this course has progressed, I have really — honestly, I have lost respect. I really loved his work. I thought he had some really great stuff. All of it is AI-generated.

To the point where we got our first grade last week. Our work was graded for using AI [correction: graded with AI]. He gave me a one-sentence comment that didn't even match my grade, and the rubric was changed from the rubric that he gave us.
The crazy part was — the AI actually caught work [mistakes] that he didn't catch in my [content]. That's how I know he used the AI to grade it.

Now I'm conflicted — because at least the AI caught something and gave me points for it that you didn't. But it's because you couldn't take two minutes to even look through my work that you begged for.
No — this is my third.

I have found in my classes, it's a little frustrating. Beforehand, I — prefer to not use it, as little as possible. My peers who are using it more, and they're better at using AI than I am — they have good projects. I'm not going to take that away.

But I recognize when somebody's using AI, and I'm sure our professors do as well. It's frustrating, because obviously that's the era we're getting into. I know that was a prompt versus I'm putting in real work. And this is the era we're getting into, and I just don't know how to perceive that.
On one hand, I know what it is. On the other hand, I'm like, "okay, their project is better in [my] mind than [mine]."
I have noticed that since I've been here, we have been implementing design less — because there's been a heavier focus on AI.
Since I left undergrad and came here, I have noticed that I have not been able to practice my design as much, and I am losing that — because I'm trying to learn how to [use AI].

That is pissing me off, because I spent four years learning design principles and building those practices. That is not cool. I am not okay with that, and that is something that I will be changing — because I am a designer. I am an artist, and that is what I am in school for. Not to become an AI generator.

Honestly — I think we will be purposely talking about AI. I don't think it was necessary. We were perfectly capable of doing research. We were perfectly capable of animating. We were perfectly capable of creating games.
One of my biggest issues is that all of these processes — animating, graphic design, UI/UX, creating games, game design — these are such beautiful, time-consuming processes.
These human experiences deserve to take time. They are beautiful in that aspect — because they took time because they needed to. That detail was meant to be there.
And now that we're taking that away — some of these AIs are good enough that you can prompt it, and it's giving you a good output. But you know what it's lacking? The human connection.

Nobody sat down and actually created that monster from their imagination because they were like: "This is cool. I want this to be the funkiest, buoy-est, gooiest, craziest monster that I can think of, and I want to make people think back to when they were a child and had all of these crazy dreams. I want them to be immersed in this world."

I think honestly, a lot of the artists who do stick back and take the time to still create — I think they're going to make it. And I think a lot of us are scared to do that — me, one of them — because it takes time, and we're scared that this new technology is going to just run us right over.
Is it exclusive, though? Well — then you shouldn't be able [to]. You shouldn't be doing it if you can't do the 3D modeling or the engineering work.
I'm trying to figure out how I can learn how to code. There are online resources, too — like Coding Train. There was another one, I can't remember off the top of my head right now.
I want to be a professor at the end of my career.

I love knowledge. I believe in learning. I believe in education. I think education is the biggest tool you can have. I think it's so important. I will always die on the hill that you should educate yourself. You should learn.

I didn't — 3D modeling scared the hell out of me. I never thought I could be a digital artist when I was in undergrad. I changed my major my sophomore year into Fine Arts — or Studio Arts. I wasn't even digital media yet.

I took one class, tried a computer-design [class]. It was a mix of everything — it was digital, or it was graphic design. We did one project graphic design, one project 3D modeling, and one project for a game-design character. That got me into everything.

I will always be the biggest advocate — if I can do it, anyone can do it. I do think you can learn whatever you put your mind to. It's never too late. You've always got time. We have so many resources. YouTube University is such a thing. There are just so many videos.

The one thing that I learned in undergrad: no one can ever take your knowledge away from you. Your education is the one thing that you always have — whether it comes from you or an institution. I will always die on that hill.

I believe in AI as a tool. That is the only thing that's ever made me okay with it. If I can find a way for it to teach me something, I'm okay with it. It doesn't make me feel good still — because I don't even like that it [hurts third parties?] [unclear].
I think so, honestly. Yeah.

My friend is doing [a presentation] today. One thing she dove into with her research was the different factors that cause students to make the decision to use AI. One is deadline pressure — how busy their schedules are. Then their peers around them — how many peers around them are using AI. Then what classes are using AI versus what classes are not allowing them to use AI. Then the lack of clarity of whether it's okay to use or whether it's not okay to use.
All of these factors pressure people to make their own decisions — so then ethics gets left out of it.
It's an ethical center. And it has to be of personal volition to choose not to —

It's been going for so long now, and there's no regulations around it. And the more they keep pushing it, the more people are okay with it. And the more people are okay with it, the further they're going to keep pushing it.
In San Francisco, they just opened a store that is run by the AI.

I got a job offer out on LinkedIn, [I thought it was for] monitoring the AI. No — it's the manager of the store. That's crazy. Real people applied to the job, and then they had an interview, and then they asked the AI: "Am I going to talk to a human at any point?" And [the AI] was like, "No." And they work for this AI in this store that picked out all of the clothes, the hats, all of the supplies that they sell. It's in San Francisco. It's insane. All deferred to AI.
I'm not teaching thesis anymore. Actually — I teach thesis sometimes.

In terms of thesis development — students can rely so heavily on generative AI that they don't actually really think through what they're doing, and what they need to be doing, which is choosing theories or theoretical frameworks that they can actually tie to their design choices.
They don't necessarily understand what those theories are and how they apply — because they're utilizing generative AI to figure that out for them.
There's sort of like a flatness that's happening.
No friction. There's a very little friction in the learning.
I've heard from other professors that — just even having students, like, undergraduate students watch a two-minute video and have a dialogue around it — is almost impossible.
Very few people are spending time actually taking something small, short, that they can watch, and having conversations around it afterwards.
Being able to actually even answer new questions becomes difficult if you're always relying on some other thing to answer questions for you.
It's like they're offloading thinking.
I would say that in our courses — I think that, particularly for non-English speakers, there's a lot of beautiful words generated by AI.
I'm not getting any sense that when people come up and they're reading those that they're their words at all — or that they necessarily even understand the words.
They're translating into English, but from English, they're not translating it back and seeing if it makes — the time really understanding what the translation means.
That naturally, unfortunately, leads to offloading of their own thinking.
It feels very false. There's a lot of falseness in it — like, it doesn't feel like I'm getting any sense of who this person is.
Yeah — as an artist.
Well, I think what we're doing is actually different than just design thinking.

We're trying to build stuff and put it in front of people, so that the real data is — not like we can build something, and we can vibe-code it, or whatever — but we need to put it in front of someone and actually see if it's helping to solve.

When we talk about, like, Discovery — or, you know, sort of like doing that sort of, like, defining, or empathizing — that's great, but that doesn't necessarily translate at all into the choices that a designer makes.
The only way you can really see if it translates is if you put it in front.

When you design a game — it's really bad when you start. Until you put it in front of people, and they're willing to play it. And then every time you play it, you can get better and better and better at making small changes to it.
We want to get to building — but not for the sake of building. We want to get to building for the sake of actually doing research and understanding.
The design is the hypothesis.
I think it's almost impossible to monitor and manage it, and it's very scary, as, like, thinking about from an administrator's perspective.
We're just slowly watching a train wreck.
We still need people who know how to program, how to deal with security, and I think that those are things that are not going to go away.
From my perspective, I use AI like a research assistant.
It helps me do really, really, really good thinking. Based off of your previously, you know, forged thinking before.
It helps me really think through loose ideas that I have into more developed ideas. Points me to greater research.
I think it's great if you're willing to be the one in control, and you're willing to have the ideas. I think that it's phenomenal.
I do know that there's this one tool that a Stanford design school professor created — and it's called — I forget what it is — but it's a reflection bot.
I really love that, and I really would like to be using it — and having other professors use it.
It's basically just a tool where it's forcing the person interacting with it to actually have a conversation and think through, like, a reading, or something like that.
It's not just giving you answers. From Socratic method.
I think that's the kind of thing where I think that that's really, really brilliant. And we should be pursuing those things.
It's creating a lot of mush, and people are feeling like everything is super derivative, because it's just using all the rules that are out there and just repurposing.
It gets talked about a lot. A lot of people are very negative about it. Actually, most people are negative about it.
They've accepted the fact that they're going to have to incorporate it into their curriculums, which seems weird.
The question is: what has prepared me?
Whatever the tool is today is not going to be the tool tomorrow, so you need to be a good thinker to figure it out.
Process, and the thinking, that goes into the artifact.

That's why — you know, blogs, or, like, developer blogs, or process journals — all of those things about the choices that we make at different stages — that's where it becomes really essential in a place like this.
I went to BYU-Idaho, and did my degree in communications with an emphasis in video production.
I think the immersive side is, like, as far as protected from AI — I would say it's pretty safe, because there's so much that has to be done at the human level.
The interaction has to be from a human standpoint.

When I was getting into my degree with Motion Media, it hadn't really even started yet. This was back in 2023, so it was at the very early stages — like, the images it was creating were all right, but then the videos were really awful, like a spaghetti monster almost.

I do use AI in my workflow sometimes. I'll use it for paintings and paint-outs — like if I need to have a shot look a certain way, or have it do something specific, then I can kind of tailor it using ComfyUI.
With AI, from my standpoint, it's not necessarily something to get a final product — it's more something to conceptualize and iterate quickly.

When you try to use AI for a final deliverable, you might save a lot of time at the front end — where you can iterate and get things done quickly and get through approvals — but as soon as it gets to the point where you need to art-direct it, it's impossible.
You will spend hours upon hours just trying to do a simple change, because of the nature of how AI is set up: the math behind it is inherently chaotic and random.
There's always going to be that level of chaotic dissonance essentially involved in every generation. Trying to control that — it's just not really possible.

When I was at SCAD is kind of when I first started playing around with AI. I had a lot of professors — Nye was one of them — that encouraged us to look into AI and the different avenues and what it can do.
The more important thing isn't necessarily what it can do. It's what it can't do.
Playing around and getting to know the AI, or the different models, is important because it's being able to articulate and understand what it can't do rather than what it can do.
That was really beneficial when I was at SCAD — having that understanding and that guidance: this is an important thing, it's not going to go away, so you might as well learn and acclimate to it.
The important thing is being able to disconnect the marketing from the reality — because the way that things are marketed is not accurate at all to what AI is actually capable of.

On February 21, 2023, the U.S. Copyright Office ruled regarding Kristina Kashtanova's graphic novel Zarya of the Dawn (created using Midjourney) that Kashtanova's original text and her 'selection, coordination, and arrangement' of the visual and written elements were protected.

The U.S. Copyright Office ruled that the individual AI-generated images in Zarya of the Dawn were not protected because 'a person who provides text prompts to Midjourney does not actually form the generated images.'

The Copyright Office reasoned that Midjourney 'begins the image generation process with a field of visual noise, which is refined based on tokens created from user prompts' and 'the prompt text does not dictate a specific result.'

The Copyright Office published formal guidance effective March 16, 2023 establishing that human authorship is required to register a work and that if a work contains more than a de minimis amount of AI-generated material, applicants must disclose that information and describe the human author's contribution.

In August 2023, the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia upheld the Copyright Office's denial of registration for 'A Recent Entrance to Paradise,' a work generated by Stephen Thaler's AI system DABUS (listed as sole author), holding that human authorship is a bedrock requirement of copyright.
On January 29, 2025, the Copyright Office released 'Copyright and Artificial Intelligence, Part 2: Copyrightability,' its most comprehensive analysis to date.
The Copyright Office Part 2 Report states 'Copyright law protects only works of human creation.'

The Copyright Office Part 2 Report concludes 'Given current generally available technology, prompts alone do not provide sufficient human control to make users of an AI system the authors of the output.'

The Copyright Office Part 2 Report states 'What matters is the extent to which the human had creative control over the work's expression. When AI determines the expressive elements of its output, the generated material is not the product of human authorship.'

The Copyright Office Part 2 Report states 'Using AI to help create a work does not necessarily undermine copyrightability.' Human authors are entitled to copyright in 'their works of authorship that are perceptible in AI-generated outputs, as well as the creative selection, coordination, or arrangement of material in the outputs, or creative modifications of the outputs.'

On March 18, 2025, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit unanimously affirmed the district court, holding that 'the Copyright Act of 1976 requires all eligible work to be authored in the first instance by a human being.'
The D.C. Circuit held the Copyright Act's 'text, taken as a whole, is best read as making humanity a necessary condition for authorship.'
The D.C. Circuit reasoned that ownership is based on the author's legal ability to hold property, and 'machines cannot own property.'

The D.C. Circuit noted that the human authorship requirement 'still incentivizes humans like Dr. Thaler to create and to pursue exclusive rights to works that they make with the assistance of artificial intelligence.'
The D.C. Circuit did not address whether the Constitution itself requires human authorship.
On March 2, 2026, the U.S. Supreme Court declined without comment to hear Thaler's petition for certiorari, leaving the D.C. Circuit's human authorship requirement intact.

Jason Allen is challenging the Copyright Office's refusal to register 'Theatre D'opera Spatial,' created using Midjourney through 624 iterative prompts, then upscaled with Gigapixel AI and retouched in Photoshop; a Motion for Summary Judgment was filed in August 2025 with no final ruling as of April 2026.
Allen argues he 'selected the colors, the style, and the era of the artwork, and arranged the elements in the image.'

The Allen v. Perlmutter case is more significant than Thaler for MFA thesis assessment because it tests the question of degree of human involvement -- whether extensive prompt engineering, iteration, and post-processing constitute sufficient human authorship.
Lemley & Ouellette state 'With rare exceptions, generative AI doesn't just copy someone else's creative expression.'

Lemley & Ouellette state 'Students and others who use AI to produce their work generally aren't engaged in copyright infringement, but they are often passing someone else's work off as their own, whether or not they know it.'
Lemley & Ouellette argue 'The growing problem of AI-facilitated plagiarism should be addressed through the extralegal norms and academic sanctions that have long governed these kinds of concerns.'
Lemley & Ouellette draw a sharp distinction between the legal question (copyright) and the academic question (plagiarism/integrity), arguing they require different frameworks.

Harvard Law Review (2025) interrogates the 'double bind' AI creates for artistic communities: the urge to use a new tool for greater creativity while that tool simultaneously threatens the human artist with irrelevance.

Mantegna (Yale Law Journal Forum, 2024) argues that 'overreaching copyright laws will negatively impact society and the development of ethical AI' and that expansion of copyright doctrine 'has proven to increase the complexity and uncertainty of copyright doctrine's application -- ironically leading to the stifling of innovation.'

El Khoury (2025) traces the evolution of higher education's response to generative AI through seven 'waves,' from initial panic and ban-oriented responses to more nuanced integration, documenting the shift from detection-focused strategies to assessment redesign.

Frontiers in Artificial Intelligence (2026) documents a pragmatic shift in the literature toward 'authenticity and process evidence: oral/practical examinations, competency-based evaluations, portfolios, and designs that make metacognition visible.'

JLDHE (2024/2025) argues that when students must articulate their understanding in real-time conversations, explain their reasoning, respond to unanticipated questions, or defend their conclusions against challenges, they demonstrate intellectual ownership that is difficult to fake.

Zailuddin et al. (2024) find that AI integration 'signals the onset of a new era in technological empowerment in creative education' while emphasizing 'the irreplaceable value of human mentorship in cultivating creativity and advancing analytical thinking.'

UNESCO (2025) argues for a fundamental rethinking of assessment toward 'continuous, portfolio-based evaluations that reflect sustained development of competencies over time, which would resist AI replication and provide richer predictive information about student capabilities.'

Inside Higher Ed (2025) reports growing consensus that detection-based approaches are failing and that assessment redesign (oral defenses, process portfolios, collaborative projects, AI co-authored writing with reflection) is the viable path forward.

Targeted searches of Design Studies and the International Journal of Art & Design Education (iJADE) for papers specifically on AI assessment in design student work returned limited results; the field most disrupted by generative AI has produced the least assessment-specific scholarship.
The NEA (National Education Association, distinct from NAEA) adopted a broader policy statement on AI in education in July 2024.
NEA policy states AI tools must be reassessed regularly by educators and that AI should only be adopted 'once there is data supporting a tool's appropriateness and efficacy.'
NEA policy states AI must not 'subject students to higher surveillance than their peers or create an over-reliance on content and assessment delivered by AI-enhanced technology.'
Policies exist at the institutional and course level, but thesis evaluation -- the highest-stakes assessment in an MFA -- operates in a policy vacuum.

The legal framework (copyright) and the academic framework (integrity/mastery) are misaligned: copyright law asks 'who controlled the expression?' while academic assessment asks 'what has the student mastered?'

If AI-generated portions of a work are not copyrightable, then a thesis containing substantial AI-generated material is, in copyright terms, partially in the public domain; the student cannot claim legal authorship of those portions.

The Copyright Office standard 'creative control over the work's expression' maps directly onto what a thesis committee might evaluate: did the student exercise creative judgment, or did the student delegate creative decisions to the AI?

The Zarya of the Dawn precedent suggests that selection, arrangement, and curation of AI-generated elements may constitute original authorship, providing a framework for evaluating thesis work that uses AI.

Lemley & Ouellette's distinction between copyright (legal) and plagiarism (normative) suggests that even if AI-assisted work does not infringe copyright, it may still violate academic integrity norms if the student claims the AI's creative contribution as their own.

R1 loop structure: AI detection tools deployed --> false positives and invasive monitoring --> student trust erodes --> students adopt evasion tools (humanizers) --> institutions deploy more aggressive detection --> trust erodes further --> cycle accelerates.

R1 is a reinforcing (positive) feedback loop in Meadows' terminology -- a vicious cycle where each intervention amplifies the problem it was designed to solve; it also exhibits Meadows' "policy resistance" system trap.

AI "humanizer" tools (Smodin AI Humanizer, Undetectable AI, uPass AI) promise to transform ChatGPT output into text that "passes any detector" by shuffling syntax, injecting idiomatic phrasing, and intentionally raising entropy to mimic human spontaneity.
Student forums contain hundreds of walkthroughs explaining how to draft in a generator, paste into a humanizer, and submit through Turnitin.
In 2025, Turnitin announced new "AI bypasser detection" capabilities specifically designed to detect text modified by humanizer tools -- an escalation that further entrenches the adversarial dynamic.
NBC News reported that some students who never used AI for writing are now running their own work through humanizers to avoid false accusations -- a direct indicator of trust collapse.

GPTZero's founder has publicly acknowledged the arms race may be unwinnable using current technological approaches, suggesting institutions need to rethink their entire approach to assignments and assessment rather than relying on detection.

Jisc (UK higher education body) frames the dynamic explicitly as a "classic cat-and-mouse game," noting that one of the earliest and most common strategies is paraphrasing tools like Quillbot to modify AI-generated text to evade detection.
Studies emphasize that excessive reliance on AI detection fosters a "culture of suspicion rather than support," where the pedagogical relationship becomes adversarial.

Jisc calculated that even a 1% false positive rate would generate approximately 4,800 false positives annually at a mid-sized institution -- "a huge burden to investigate and manage and potentially damaging for student trust and wellbeing."
Australian Catholic University (ACU) reported nearly 6,000 cases of alleged cheating in 2024, with approximately 90% related to AI use.
One ACU paramedic student's essay was flagged as 84% AI-generated; students had transcripts marked "results withheld" for six months, preventing entry into professional fields like nursing.
ACU stopped using the Turnitin AI detector in March 2024 after being aware of the tool's problems for over a year.

French national Thierry Rignol, a Yale SOM EMBA student, sued Yale after being suspended for one year for alleged AI use on a final exam; his lawsuit alleges he was coerced into a false confession, denied due process, and discriminated against as a non-native English speaker. The case remains active as of 2026.

PhD student Haishan Yang was expelled from the University of Minnesota Health Services Research program after faculty accused him of using AI on a qualifying exam; he filed a federal lawsuit and human rights complaint alleging discrimination based on national origin. The federal court dismissed his suit in October 2025, and the Minnesota Court of Appeals affirmed the university's decision in February 2026.
R2 loop structure: students use AI for cognitive tasks --> less practice with independent reasoning --> reduced skill/confidence --> increased dependence on AI --> further skill atrophy.
R2 is a reinforcing loop that maps to Meadows' "drift to low performance" system trap, where the system's performance standard erodes gradually as actors accept lower benchmarks.

A systematic review of empirical research published between 2023 and 2025 found that while AI enhances personalized learning, excessive reliance may reduce cognitive engagement and long-term retention; prolonged AI exposure led to memory decline in one study of 73 information science undergraduates.

The Cognitive Paradox authors note: "the quantitative evidence for enhancement is currently far more substantial and systematically documented than the evidence for cognitive dependence, which often remains an identified risk or a theoretical concern rather than a consistently measured outcome."

A mixed-methods study of 666 participants found a significant negative correlation between frequent AI tool usage and critical thinking abilities, mediated by increased cognitive offloading; younger participants exhibited higher dependence on AI and lower critical thinking scores compared to older participants.

Using data from 580 university students, researchers found that greater AI dependence was associated with lower levels of critical thinking, with cognitive fatigue partially mediating this relationship; information literacy served as a moderating factor.

An empirical study from China found that AI dependence negatively impacts college students' innovation capability, identifying both tool dependence (relying on functional assistance) and cognitive dependence (relying on AI to replace independent thinking in high-level cognitive activities).
GenAI dependency negatively mediates the relationship between AI use and academic achievement through reduced self-efficacy.
A study involving 1,276 participants from 76 countries identified urgency for regulatory evolution, as generative AI "may have a negative relation with creative thinking skills in the long run."

A quasi-experimental study over 12 weeks with 240 participants found that structured AI-enabled cognitive offload instruction actually produced greater improvements in critical thinking assessments and higher-quality essays; the key variable was pedagogical design.

The leverage point is not whether AI is used but how it is integrated pedagogically -- a Meadows-level intervention at the "rules of the system" (leverage point 5) rather than the "parameters" level (leverage point 12).

R3 loop structure: AI enables students to produce passable work without learning --> institutions deploy detection tools --> detection tools prove unreliable --> students adopt evasion tools --> detection companies escalate technology --> evasion tools escalate in response --> institutions spend more on detection --> fundamental assessment validity continues to decline.
R3 maps to Meadows' "escalation" system trap -- two parties (detection companies and evasion tool developers) locked in a competitive spiral that degrades the system for everyone else.
89% of students admit to leaning on generative AI for at least part of their coursework.
AI-related academic misconduct now represents 60-64% of all cheating cases in higher education institutions globally as of 2025.

86% of students reported using AI in their studies in the Digital Education Council's 2024 global survey of 3,800+ students across 16 countries; only 5% were fully aware of their institution's AI guidelines.
Success rates of humanizer tools hover around 70-80% in evading detection across independent tests.
A 2024 study by Perkins et al. revealed AI detection rates dropping from 39.5% to 17.4% after basic adversarial modifications were applied.
A 2023 study testing 14 AI detectors found most scored below 80% accuracy; overall accuracy reached only 27.9% in some conditions; paraphrased texts pushed the undetected rate to roughly 50%.

California universities alone spent over $15 million on Turnitin purchases, with per-student pricing ranging from $1.79 to $6.50 for core plagiarism detection; Turnitin charges some schools 360% more than others.
The California State University System spent $1.1 million in 2025, with an additional $163,000 specifically for the AI detection add-on.
OpenAI discontinued its own AI detector after finding it correctly identified only 26% of AI-written text while falsely flagging 9% of human writing.

Katsamakas, Pavlov, and Saklad (2024), "Artificial Intelligence and the Transformation of Higher Education Institutions: A Systems Approach" (MDPI Sustainability), develops a causal loop diagram (CLD) mapping the feedback mechanisms of AI transformation in higher education, identifying reinforcing and balancing loops between technological advancement, pedagogical methodology, institutional structure, and societal factors.

AI investment creates reinforcing loops in student learning and research productivity, while simultaneously generating balancing loops through academic integrity challenges and job market disruption; AI "can bring substantial restructuring by creating new feedback loops, rewiring existing ones, and strengthening or weakening others."

Corbin, Dawson, and Liu (2025) distinguish discursive changes (modifications that rely on communicating rules, e.g., "traffic light" systems for AI use permissions) from structural changes (modifications that reshape the underlying mechanics of assessment tasks themselves, e.g., oral defenses, real-time problem-solving, iterative assessments with documented process).
Discursive changes create an "enforcement illusion" -- borrowing language from familiar structural systems while lacking their enforcement capabilities.

Current institutional approaches predominantly rely on discursive changes that cannot ensure assessment validity; only structural redesign -- building validity into assessment architecture -- can address the fundamental challenge AI poses to assessment.

Stanford's Hasso Plattner Institute of Design (d.school) has piloted process documentation approaches in select courses where students submit drafts, annotations, and reflective journals alongside final work, capturing "the writing journey -- how drafts evolved, where revisions occurred, what the pacing and engagement looked like across the session" -- creating a verifiable record of authorship that does not rely on probabilistic inference.
Stanford's Academic Integrity Working Group (2025) recommended in-person assessment formats such as oral exams and in-class writing assignments for high-stakes assessments where AI use is restricted.
University of Oxford (2024) revised its Academic Integrity Framework to explicitly shift from detection-first approaches toward assessment redesign and transparent disclosure policies.

Oral defenses must move "from confirmatory questions that permit regurgitated responses to exploratory inquiry that demonstrates genuine conceptual transformation"; students are evaluated in real-time, making AI-assisted cheating difficult or impossible.
Inside Higher Ed reported that blue books "made a comeback in 2025," with professors asking students to write in-person in traditional examination booklets.

Process portfolios with reflection journals require students to document their iterative creative process, including false starts, revisions, and reflective commentary on decisions, creating an evidence trail that is difficult to fabricate with AI.

At SCAD, illustration and sequential art faculty expressed strong opposition to AI integration, with professors noting: "I can't make a graphic novel with AI because the publishing industry will never accept it."
Nye Warburton, who leads SCAD's Applied AI program, acknowledged: "I'm not a very popular human being in certain majors."

Education law attorneys have documented a pattern of faculty over-reliance on AI detection tools leading to wrongful accusations, describing it as "hysteria" that undermines pedagogical relationships.

EDUCAUSE 2025 found a marked increase in enthusiasm for AI and a slight decrease in apprehensive attitudes from 2024 to 2025; 81% of respondents feel enthusiasm or a mix of caution and enthusiasm, while 17% reported feeling cautious or very cautious.
Two-thirds (68%) reported that students use AI "somewhat more" or "a lot more" than faculty, indicating an adoption gap.

UNESCO Survey 2025 (400 responses from UNESCO Chairs and UNITWIN Networks across 90 countries): nine in ten respondents use AI tools professionally (most commonly for research and writing), and nearly half experiment with AI in teaching; over half feel uncertain or hesitant about effective pedagogical or research application.
Only 2% of institutions accommodate new AI-related costs through new funding sources; a plurality of executive leaders (34%) said their institutions underestimated AI-related costs.

A case-study analysis of three creative technology courses (production design, fine arts, digital artistry) found that AI integration "signals the onset of a new era in technological empowerment in creative education"; AI tools including DALL-E and Wombo Dream were instrumental in "bolstering creative ideation, with students able to traverse previously insurmountable creative barriers and produce a plethora of ideas in reduced timeframes."
The same study emphasized "the irreplaceable value of human mentorship in cultivating creativity and advancing analytical thinking."
Creative tasks relying on human intuition and divergent thinking "may be stifled by systematic AI tools."

Industrial design, UX, architecture, and interior design departments at SCAD are described as "proactively moving forward in AI" with "a clear idea of how they can integrate it into their processes"; photography faculty were characterized as "already disrupted by digital, so they're kind of ready for [AI]."
Around 70% of institutions in Europe and North America have or are developing AI guidance, versus 45% in Latin America and the Caribbean.

A critical analysis (Taylor & Francis, 2025) argued that UNESCO's policy constitutes "techno-solutionism" -- framing AI as both the problem and the solution while inadequately addressing structural inequalities.
Turnitin self-reports 98% accuracy with <1% false positive rate for text containing at least 20% AI writing.
Turnitin's product officer acknowledged the company intentionally finds about 85% of AI-generated content while letting 15% pass in order to reduce false positives to <1%.
Independent testing found false positive rates of 10-15% in diverse educational settings -- substantially higher than Turnitin's claims.

GPTZero accuracy is up to 96% for essays in academic settings; drops to 78% on texts under 200 words; 2% false positive rate across all content types; claims 100% detection on GPT-5 output and 94.9% on GPT-5-mini (2026 benchmarks).

Originality.ai self-reports 99% accuracy with 0.5% false positive rate (Lite model), but catches only 7.3% of GPT-5-mini output as of 2026, meaning it misses nearly everything from the most popular current OpenAI model.
OpenAI's discontinued classifier had a 9% false positive rate and 74% false negative rate.
Stanford Study: AI detectors were "near-perfect" with essays by U.S.-born eighth-graders but misclassified over 61% of essays written by non-native English speakers as AI-generated.
ESL submissions are up to 30% more likely to be falsely flagged compared to native speakers.
Common Sense Media (2024) found that Black students are more likely to be falsely accused of AI-generated writing by their teachers.
Neurodiverse students also face higher false-positive rates due to writing patterns that differ from "typical" human writing.

Turnitin published an internal study testing nearly 2,000 ELL writing samples, concluding no statistically significant bias (0.014 FP rate for ELL vs. 0.013 for native speakers); however, every independent study contradicts this finding.

At least 12 major universities have disabled or abandoned AI detection features entirely, including Vanderbilt (Aug 2023), Yale (prohibits GPTZero), Johns Hopkins, Northwestern, UT Austin (banned purchases 2024), UCLA, UC San Diego, Cal State LA, University of Waterloo, ACU Australia (March 2024), University of Minnesota, Penn State, Michigan State.

In a university with 20,000 students, a 1-5% false positive rate generates 200-1,000 wrongful accusations per semester -- each requiring investigation, causing stress, and potentially resulting in permanent academic record damage.

R4 loop: well-resourced institutions adopt AI effectively --> better outcomes --> more resources --> better AI integration; under-resourced institutions lack AI infrastructure --> worse outcomes --> fewer resources --> wider gap; students with premium AI tool access (GPT-4, Claude) outperform those limited to free tools or no access.
B1 loop: AI disrupts assessment --> faculty redesign assessments (oral, process-based) --> assessment validity restored --> student learning measured authentically.
B2 loop: harm cases accumulate --> institutions abandon detection --> investment shifts to pedagogy --> assessment redesign --> reduced harm.
B3 loop: AI dependence harms learning --> awareness grows --> AI literacy programs develop --> structured AI use --> learning outcomes improve.

Detection-based approaches face policy resistance because every actor in the system has rational reasons to subvert the policy: students evade detection to protect grades; faculty rely on detection to manage workload; detection companies profit from escalation; evasion companies profit from counter-escalation; the policy defeats itself.
As AI produces "good enough" work, assessment standards may gradually accommodate AI-level output rather than human-level mastery; the system redefines "acceptable" downward.

The detection-evasion arms race is a textbook escalation trap: each side's response to the other's move becomes the trigger for the next move; the only escape is to refuse to play -- which is exactly what institutions abandoning detection are doing.

AI adoption advantages compound: well-funded institutions can invest in pedagogical redesign; under-funded ones are stuck with broken detection tools they cannot afford to replace with better approaches.
Shift from "AI as cheating tool to be detected" to "AI as medium to be mastered"; institutions that have made this shift (like SCAD's Applied AI program) report fundamentally different dynamics.
Shift the goal from "verify authentic individual authorship" to "develop demonstrable competence through documented process"; this changes what gets measured and rewarded.
Structural assessment redesign (Corbin et al. 2025) -- changing the mechanics of how assessment works rather than the rules around prohibited behavior.

Process documentation (Stanford d.school model) creates new information flows that make the learning process visible; this is more effective than detection because it generates positive information rather than policing negative behavior.

The current system has dangerous delays: AI adoption is rapid (months); institutional policy response is slow (years); faculty training is slower; assessment redesign is slowest. These mismatched time constants create the chaotic period currently observed.
Adjusting detection thresholds, tweaking AI tool permissions, updating syllabi language -- most current institutional responses operate at this level, which is precisely why they are ineffective.
AACE reports that three assessment categories have emerged -- traditional, innovative/refocused, and GenAI-incorporated -- but "widespread adoption of AI-driven teaching approaches remains limited."
Process-based assessment is significantly more labor-intensive for faculty, creating a resource constraint that limits scalability.

Oral defenses are already standard in many graduate programs, making the transition more natural at this level; MFA programs typically require exhibition or portfolio presentation, written thesis or artist statement, and oral defense before a committee.
The AI challenge at the MFA level is primarily in the written components and in whether process work (sketches, iterations, documented development) authentically represents the student's journey.
EDUCAUSE 2025: 57% view AI as strategic priority (up from 49% in 2024).
Digital Education Council 2024: 80% of 3,800+ students across 16 countries say AI in universities is not meeting expectations.
Washington Post test recorded 50% false positive rate for Turnitin (small sample).

Vallor (2024, The AI Mirror) deploys the metaphor of AI as a 'mirror'—reflecting our intelligence, biases, and desires back at us—to diagnose how we are going wrong in our relationship with the technology.
Vallor's central warning is the growing risk of moral deskilling: the progressive outsourcing of ethical judgments and practical decisions to systems incapable of moral reasoning.
Vallor (echoing Aristotle): 'excessive reliance on these machines will stunt our practical wisdom which … is a skill that requires, and is developed through, exercise.'
Vallor names autofabrication as a deeper existential risk—'not AI's autonomy, but our own progressive erosion of moral confidence, agency, and ambition.'

Vallor (2016, Technology and the Virtues) argues that technologies can both enable and impede the development of virtues like honesty, patience, and empathy, and urges builders to 'create technologies that help cultivate human virtues rather than hinder them.'

For creative education, Vallor's framework demands asking not only 'Can the student produce good work?' but 'Does the process of education cultivate the virtues necessary for sustained creative practice?'

Sennett (2008, The Craftsman) defines craftsmanship as 'the basic human impulse to do a job well for its own sake,' requiring 'material consciousness' combined with years of practice and a 'strategic acceptance of ambiguity.'
Sennett: 'All skills, even the more abstract, begin as bodily practices'—creative mastery is not purely cognitive but somatically encoded.

Sennett: any algorithmic solution to a crafting problem 'cannot itself be generated algorithmically, as it must include ad hoc constraints known only through practice—through embodied manipulations,' placing a theoretical limit on automation.

Ian's synthesis of Sennett: what AI cannot replicate is not the output of creative mastery but the formation of the practitioner—the embodied, iterative, failure-rich process through which judgment and taste are cultivated.
Crawford (2009, Shop Class as Soulcraft) argues against 'a misguided separation of thinking from doing.'

Crawford contends tacit knowledge—the kind of expertise a mechanic develops through years of diagnosing engines—'goes beyond explicit rules and representations' and 'cannot be readily made explicit or formalized.'

Crawford: the crafting problem involves 'ad hoc constraints known only through practice,' which 'places a theoretical limit on the automation of work'; experience enables 'intuitive judgments that algorithms often cannot replicate.'
The Dreyfus model (Dreyfus & Dreyfus, 1986) describes five stages of skill acquisition: novice, advanced beginner, competent, proficient, and expert.

Dreyfus: 'When things are proceeding normally, experts don't solve problems and don't make decisions; they do what normally works'—expert performance is rapid, intuitive, pattern-based, not deliberate rule-following.
Polanyi (1966): 'We can know more than we can tell.' Tacit knowledge is acquired through practical experience and is subjective and contextual.
For creative mastery, the most important knowledge a practitioner possesses is precisely the knowledge that resists codification—and therefore resists direct transfer to or from an AI system.

Recent analysis: 'the interaction process with AI is itself a reflection of human tacit knowledge—how we choose to phrase a task, what examples we give, and which assumptions we clarify all stem from human intuition'; AI use may require tacit expertise rather than replacing it.

A 2025 CACM article 'Polanyi's Revenge and AI's New Romance with Tacit Knowledge' argues modern AI systems have side-stepped rather than solved Dreyfus's challenges—evading constraints through statistical pattern-matching rather than achieving genuine understanding.
Steyerl (2025, Medium Hot) argues AI-generated images are produced 'as if by unmediated magic' when their actual source is 'massive exploitation and expropriation at the level of production.'
Steyerl warns creative workers risk becoming dependent on 'proprietary pipelines,' with their ability to work linked to big tech companies like Adobe and Google.

Steyerl's 'Mean Images' demonstrates 'data populism' as encoded social bias—a prompt for 'protest' producing images focused exclusively on riot police; she uses 'artificial stupidity' to counter overrated AI expectations.
Paglen investigates 'what it means to make images when representation is no longer primarily a site for construction of meaning by humans but also a field of data for analysis by machines.'

Manovich & Arielli (Artificial Aesthetics, 2024/25): 'AI image tools are much better at generating visuals of popular subjects and aesthetics than unfamiliar or rare ones,' revealing a regression to the aesthetic mean.
When prompted for unfamiliar content, AI tools 'either produce lower-quality results … or substitute requested content with more commonplace alternatives, generating more generic (cliche) elements.'
Manovich frames AI as 'an augmentation of our aesthetic skills, deepening both our creative processes and our understanding and sensibility of cultural artifacts.'
Ian's synthesis: AI is a tool for competent mediocrity, not for the kind of aesthetic risk-taking that defines breakthrough creative work.
Kate Crawford (2021, Atlas of AI) reveals AI's 'global networks' are 'damaging the environment, entrenching inequality, and fueling a shift toward undemocratic governance.'

Bridle (New Dark Age, 2018/2023) warns against 'the belief that quantitative data can provide a coherent model of the world'; his 2023 afterword addresses generative AI's 'wholesale appropriation of existing images stored on the internet.'

Bryson's Moral Agency Framework requires (a) clear and just human lines of accountability, (b) verifiability for humans whose work is augmented by AI, and (c) AI introduction only where it doesn't inhibit bureaucracies' twin aims of legitimacy and stewardship.
The MFA is a terminal degree qualifying holders to teach at the university level; the thesis is expected to be 'a work of publishable quality.'

If AI can generate publishable-quality creative work, the degree's certification shifts from output capacity to 'critical thinking, unique creative vision, and directorial leadership—qualities that remain distinctly human in the age of AI.'

The College Art Association's MFA guidelines emphasize studio practice, critique participation, and the ability to 'discuss their work and its influences, as well as its relationship to contemporary [practice]'—a relational and discursive competence no AI currently possesses.
Caplan (2018, The Case Against Education): 'approximately 80% of individuals' return to education is the result of signaling, with the remainder due to human capital accumulation.'
Caplan: education's primary function is not to enhance skills but to 'certify intelligence, conscientiousness, and conformity—attributes valued by employers.'

If AI collapses the output differential between MFA holders and non-holders, the signaling value of the degree erodes; a thesis that could plausibly be AI-generated signals nothing about the holder's intelligence, conscientiousness, or creative capacity.

Caplan recommends greater vocational education (Germany/Switzerland model), aligning with craft theory: if mastery is embodied and tacit, creative education should look more like apprenticeship than seminar-and-thesis.

Collins (1979/2019, The Credential Society) identified 'an unacknowledged spiral of the rising production of credentials and job requirements'; expansion of access dilutes value, driving holders back for more advanced degrees.

Collins: 'the historical trend to inflate degrees goes through periodic crises—either the students can't afford the degrees when their job payoff declines, or the government (or parents) can't afford to keep expanding the educational system.'
In 2013, 53% of Americans agreed a 4-year degree gives 'a better chance to get a good job and earn more income.' By 2023, education-believers fell to 42%, while 56% said it was not worth the cost.
AIGA launched 'AIGA Designer 2025' and Professional Design Certification, but specific public position statements on how AI changes what a design degree signals remain limited.

ACM convened a working group on 'Ethical and Societal Impacts of Generative AI in Higher Computing Education' at ITiCSE 2025; a joint study found 'insufficient evidence addressing comprehensive AI practice methodologies.'
No publicly available NASAD accreditation guidance specifically addressing generative AI in design education was found as of this research date.
IDSA held its 2024 International Design Conference & Education Symposium, but no specific public position paper on AI and design degree certification was found.

Studies found participants evaluated AI-labeled artworks as having taken less time to produce and as being less creative and worth less money; AI was rated as 'exerting less effort than humans,' correlating with negative evaluations.
'Some empirical investigations have found that AI-generated art is indistinguishable from human art in several experimental contexts.'

Recent research proposes human-centered computational frameworks linking subjective evaluations with domain-specific features, but acknowledges 'aesthetic preference depends on numerous underlying variables, like context and subjective attitudes'—capturing the surface of taste, not its depth.

Bourdieu (Distinction, 1979): 'judgments of taste are acts of social positioning'—aesthetic preferences function as markers of class, education, and cultural belonging; cultural capital determines who defines 'good taste.'

Generative AI uncouples aesthetic output from years of education and cultural immersion: 'tastes are more evenly spread across societal factions' when access to cultural knowledge is uncoupled from educational systems.

'Contemporary cultural taste is not entirely endogenous to the individual but is co-constructed through ongoing interaction with platform algorithms'; platform logics may 'unintentionally produce a new form of exclusion in knowledge mobilization.'

Scholarship identifies 'new forms of digital capital'—skills like video-editing, meme-making, live-streaming, and podcasting—that function as cultural capital in digital contexts and restructure social classes.
If MFA traditionally functioned as a site for accumulation of cultural capital distinguishing graduates' taste from non-graduates', AI threatens to flatten that distinction.
Benjamin (1936) argued technological reproduction strips art of its aura—its unique presence in time and space, its authenticity.

Kalpokas (Philosophy & Social Criticism, 2025) argues AI-generated art 'can be seen as capable of partly reversing the loss of auratic capacities that had ensued with mechanical reproduction,' via 'identification and inventive representation of data patterns' giving 'insight into the collective unconscious of the society.'
Kalpokas, Kalpokiene & Oksymets (2025) conceptualize AI-led art as 'falling in-between the Benjaminian categories of auratic art and mechanical reproduction'—a novel third category.
Park (AI & Society, 2024) investigates how generative AI 'redefines art's traditional aura while introducing a dynamic interplay between technological liberation and dependency.'
Ambrosini (2025) proposes the paradoxical notion of an 'algorithmic aura'—AI-generated artworks possess a unique form of authenticity rooted in their computational origins.

Salas Espasa & Camacho (AI & Society, 2025) introduce 'semi-aura' as a framework for AI-generated art's ambiguous authenticity, identifying polarized scholarly views on democratization vs lack of emotional depth.

Doshi & Hauser (Science Advances, 2024): 'Access to generative AI ideas causes stories to be evaluated as more creative, better written, and more enjoyable, especially among less creative writers'—less creative writers saw 10–11% creativity and 22–26% enjoyability increases.

Doshi & Hauser: 'Generative AI-enabled stories are more similar to each other than stories by humans alone.' This 'resembles a social dilemma: with generative AI, writers are individually better off, but collectively a narrower scope of novel content is produced.'
'Already creative writers showed less improvement'—AI closes the gap between skilled and unskilled rather than pushing the frontier of the skilled further forward.

Ian's synthesis: AI makes average work better but makes excellent work more homogeneous; the value of mastery (producing distinctive work) may actually increase because AI pushes everything toward the median.
A 2025 Science Advances study found individual 'masterminds' expand the creative frontier more than AI-assisted collective 'hive minds.'

'Bicycle for the mind' framing: 'When human creativity and AI capabilities merge, this generative synesthesia enables creative breakthroughs by shifting artistic focus from technical execution to ideation, curation, and refinement.'
'Photography didn't kill painting. It liberated it.' Photography 'triggered an unprecedented number of new creative and exploratory endeavors,' including Impressionism and modern art.

Critics: 'The invention of photography introduced a new medium, but it did not extract from painters to build itself.' Generative AI is built explicitly from existing human work via large-scale data collection from public websites, private portfolios, and copyrighted databases.

RISD launched Computation, Technology and Culture (CTC) department Fall 2025—its first new academic department since 1996—with focus on ethics of generative AI; courses include Generative Systems situating AI within global history of generative art and design.

Ian's synthesis: RISD represents a positive institutional vision—not banning AI or pretending it does not exist, but integrating it into a critical, historically informed, ethically grounded curriculum.

'If the final artifact becomes an unreliable indicator of student learning, the journey of development takes on greater significance.' But process documentation can itself be AI-simulated—where then does assessment anchor?
Pearson (Wonkhe): 'AI hasn't created a crisis in assessment so much as exposed an existing one'; assessment focuses on the final product, leaving the writing process invisible.
EdSource: 'Artificial intelligence isn't ruining education; it's exposing what's already broken.'

El Khoury (CUNY Assessment Review, 2025) documents the institutional response as waves: initial panic, policy creation, detection obsession, gradual redesign, with custom chatbots now serving as course assistants, tutors, process coaches, and reflective guides.

Emerging consensus: 'Authenticity cannot be policed into existence; it must be redesigned'—shift 'from what students know to how they apply knowledge, make judgement, and justify choices with AI in the loop.'
'Beyond Detection' (Education Sciences, 2025): authenticity must be 'reconceptualized as something constructed in contexts where AI is expected, declared and scrutinised.'

A processfolio asks students to depict their journey through a collection of artefacts—drafts, plans, feedback, source notes, AI prompts—accompanied by a reflection, valuing transparency, justification, and metacognition.

Critics: 'Flattening out process goes against the organic, often non-linear process of creativity'; process-based pedagogy risks 'doubl[ing] down on the product-focused mindset' by treating documentation as the product, creating a performative regime as hollow as the one it replaces.

Saunders (Substack, 2024): 'much of grading rests on the inference that a finished product reflects a student's underlying understanding. When that inference becomes shaky, assessment itself starts to feel unstable. … AI flattens differences on exactly the kinds of assignments universities have leaned on most heavily.'
Oral exams 'require real-time reasoning, application of knowledge to novel prompts, and defense of specific decisions'; structured oral formats achieve high validity and reliability.

JLDHE (2025): 'The solution to the AI world is to dramatically reweight written coursework assessments in favour of the oral defence or viva voce … with its application to undergraduate and taught postgraduate coursework being the necessary next step.'

Some institutions are exploring AI-powered oral assessment: 'Conversational AI platforms now bundle the components required for natural spoken interaction into systems good enough to conduct a structured examination'—the AI-resistance arms race may be shorter than educators hope.

Inside Higher Ed (Dec 2025): 'It's impossible to be completely certain whether a student used AI—the technology is just too good.' Recommendation: re-engage students, use class time well, introduce variety of assessments.

Cross-source consensus on what AI cannot replicate: embodied knowledge (Sennett, Crawford, Polanyi), moral/practical wisdom (Vallor), expert intuition (Dreyfus), distinctive creativity (Doshi & Hauser), aesthetic risk-taking (Manovich), relational judgment (Bourdieu).

Cross-source consensus on what AI disrupts: credentialing signals (Caplan, Collins), cultural gatekeeping (Bourdieu updated), assessment anchoring (Pearson, El Khoury), aura/authenticity (Benjamin updated), labor/extraction (Steyerl, K. Crawford).
The MFA thesis is simultaneously a credential, a process of formation, an assessment artifact, a cultural-capital instrument, and a work of art—each layer destabilized differently by AI.

Ian's framing: the question is not whether AI can produce thesis-quality work (it can) but what the thesis process produces in the person—and whether that formation is still worth the institutional, financial, and temporal investment.
